chapters.title: Unit 1: Patience and Tolerance of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)

lessons.title: Reading Notes: Patience, Tolerance and Mercy
lessons.notes_html:
The Lesson in Brief

This unit teaches patience, tolerance and mercy through four events from the life of Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH): the journey to Taif, the old woman of Makkah, the Treaty of Hudaybiyah and the Conquest of Makkah.

At Taif, the people threw stones at Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) and badly hurt him when he invited them to Islam. He did not curse them. Instead, he prayed that their future generations would turn to Islam, and his patience was later rewarded when many people of Taif accepted Islam.

An old woman in Makkah used to throw garbage on him whenever he passed her house, yet he never became angry and never fought with her. One day she did not come out, so he went to her house, found her sick and cared for her with kindness. Surprised by his good behaviour, she embraced Islam.

The Muslims were unhappy with the Treaty of Hudaybiyah because the Quraish set very difficult conditions. Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) still showed great patience and agreed to the terms for the sake of peace, and that patience later brought success to Islam.

At the Conquest of Makkah, the people feared revenge for years of cruelty, but he forgave them all and treated them with mercy instead of revenge. Thousands then accepted Islam with love and respect, and his forgiveness united the people and spread peace in Makkah.

Key Points

  • Patience means staying calm and kind even when others are cruel.
  • Forgiveness can change hearts more strongly than revenge.
  • Peace agreements may look hard at first yet bring success later.

lessons.title: Completed Sentences: Story Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Completed Sentences

  • Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) is the last Prophet of Allah.
  • At Taif, people threw stones at Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH), but he prayed for them.
  • An old woman used to throw garbage on the Prophet (PBUH), but he cared for her when she was sick.
  • At the time of the Treaty of Hudaybiyah, Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) showed patience for the sake of peace.
  • At the Conquest of Makkah, Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) forgave the people.

Each completed sentence states one fact from the lesson, so revising these sentences revises the whole story.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Types of Nouns
lessons.notes_html:
Noun Types with Worked Examples

A proper noun is the specific name of a person or place. In the worked examples, Islamabad is a proper noun because it is the specific name of a place, and Ali is a proper noun because it is the specific name of a person.

An uncountable noun names something that is measured rather than counted. The word sugar is an uncountable noun for this reason.

A collective noun names a group. The word flock is a collective noun because it names a group of sheep.

A common noun is a common name for a person or thing. The word teacher is a common noun because it is a common name for a person.

Common Gender Nouns

A common gender noun can be used for both males and females, so it does not show whether the person is male or female. The worked examples are cousin, students, friend, child and cook.

Adjectives and Verbs

An adjective describes a noun, as in the phrases old building and tall girl. A verb is an action word, as in the sentences about cooking rice and writing a story.

For picture practice, one model sentence is: a boy is climbing a tall tree. The naming words are boy and tree, the describing word is tall, and the action word is climbing.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Multi-Syllable Words and a Model Paragraph
lessons.notes_html:
Multi-Syllable Words in Sentences

  • The ambitious boy worked diligently on his project.
  • The teacher admired her respectful manner and the way she answered confidently.
  • The mysterious traveller walked silently through the forest at night.
  • The villagers praised his generosity when he gave food to the poor.
  • The courageous firefighter entered the burning house bravely.

More than one word from the bank can fit some sentences, so another fitting word is also correct. The word carefully stays unused in this model set.

Model Paragraph: My School

My school is a big, clean and beautiful place. It has many bright classrooms, a green playground and a small library full of storybooks. In the morning, the birds sing in the tall trees and the children play happily in the ground. I love my school because my teachers are kind and I learn many new things there every day.

lessons.title: Speaking Practice: At Home
lessons.notes_html:
Classroom Practice

The conversation At Home, between a mother and a son, is a speaking activity for pairs in class. It is practised aloud with polite replies, so it has no written answer. Polite, gentle replies are the habit this practice builds.

chapters.title: Unit 2: Ten Lines on Traffic Rules

lessons.title: Reading Notes: Sidra and the Traffic Rules Chart
lessons.notes_html:
The Lesson in Brief

Sidra writes ten lines about traffic rules for a class chart competition, and her teacher then teaches the whole class about traffic rules and road safety.

The teacher set a co-curricular task: every student made a chart of ten lines on an important topic to decorate the classroom. The best chart maker would receive a cash prize and a certificate.

Sidra chose traffic rules as her topic because knowing traffic rules is very important for staying safe on the road.

Three rules from her chart are: never hurry while walking on the road; always obey the traffic signals; and remember that a red light means stop, a yellow light means be ready, and a green light means go. A zebra crossing should also be used to cross the road.

Traffic rules matter because they keep order on the road and keep everyone safe while crossing roads or driving. Each year, thousands of people lose their lives on roads because someone is careless about the traffic rules.

Countries punish people who break traffic rules with harsh punishments, and in some countries a huge fine is imposed on the driver who breaks the rules.

Key Points

  • Red means stop, yellow means be ready, and green means go.
  • Roads stay safe when everyone follows the same rules.
  • Carelessness on the road costs thousands of lives every year.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Articles
lessons.notes_html:
The Rule

Use an before a vowel sound, the for a particular person or thing, and no article at all for general ideas such as music in general.

Worked Examples as Completed Sentences

  • I saw an elephant in the zoo.
  • Please give me the book on the table.
  • She bought an orange from the market.
  • I like music very much, with no article before music.
  • The sun rises in the east.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Quantifiers and Demonstratives
lessons.notes_html:
Quantifiers

Quantifiers tell how much or how many. Use many and few with countable nouns, and little with uncountable nouns.

  • There are many students in the class.
  • We have little sugar left in the jar.
  • Each boy was given a medal.
  • He has few friends in the new city.
  • All books on the shelf belong to me.

Demonstratives

Demonstratives point things out. This and these point to things near us, while that and those point to things farther away.

  • This pen in my hand is blue.
  • Those apples on the tree are red.
  • That house across the road is very old.
  • These shoes near the door are mine.
  • The car parked outside is pointed out with that.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Kinds of Adjectives and Capital Letters
lessons.notes_html:
Kinds of Adjectives

  • Two is an adjective of quantity in the phrase two pens.
  • Brave is an adjective of quality.
  • Square is an adjective of shape.
  • Red is an adjective of colour.
  • Some is an adjective of quantity in the phrase some rice.
  • Pakistani is an adjective of origin.
  • Huge is an adjective of size.

Capital Letters: Corrected Sentences

  • We will celebrate Eid tomorrow.
  • He can speak Urdu and English.
  • Dr. Ali is a good person.
  • Pakistan Resolution Day is in March.
  • My friend’s name is Ahmed Khan.

Capital letters begin a sentence and mark proper nouns such as names, languages, days and months.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Paragraph on Water Conservation
lessons.notes_html:
Model Informative Paragraph

Water is very precious for life on Earth, so we must save every drop of it. We should turn off the tap while brushing our teeth, fix leaking taps at once, and use a bucket instead of a pipe for washing. Farmers can save water by watering crops in the morning or evening, and rainwater can be stored for later use. If we all save water today, there will be enough clean water for everyone in the future.

The same informative pattern can be used for solar energy, healthy eating, the role of women in society, or recycling: state the topic, give clear facts and useful steps, and end with a hopeful closing line.

lessons.title: Speaking Practice: Observing Traffic Rules for Safety
lessons.notes_html:
Classroom Practice

The conversation Observing Traffic Rules for Safety, between Salma and Nagina, is practised aloud in class. It is a speaking activity, so it has no written answer.

lessons.title: Reading Notes: The Poem Month by Month
lessons.notes_html:
The Poem in Brief

This poem by Lucy Coates walks through the twelve months of the year and gives each month its own weather picture, from the cold winds of January to the Christmas carols of December.

January is the first month of the year. The poem calls it a new beginning, with resolutions and cold winds blowing.

February has frosty fogs, winter shivers, and logs burning warm in the fire, so February is shown as a cold, frosty winter month.

In March, the wind blows, the air smells of spring, leaves peek out, and brave blackbirds sing. March is shown as the windy start of spring.

June brings summer blazing in, with the scent of roses and the sun on the skin, so June is shown as a hot, bright summer month.

February is treated as the coldest month described in the poem because of its frosty fogs and shivering winter, with warmth coming only from fire-warmed logs. The poem itself does not name a coldest month directly, and the flags chapter at the end of this book explains this point honestly.

Key Points

  • Every month carries its own weather picture in the poem.
  • Spring begins in March and summer blazes in June.
  • Winter months are pictured with fog, frost and firelight.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Prepositions
lessons.notes_html:
The Rule

A preposition shows position, place or time and links a noun or pronoun to the rest of the sentence.

Worked Examples as Completed Sentences

  • The cat is hiding under the table.
  • She is standing at the bus stop.
  • The birds are flying over the sky.
  • He is sitting between his friends.
  • We will meet on Monday.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Noun Number and Transitional Words
lessons.notes_html:
Nouns That Keep the Same Form

Some nouns keep the same form in singular and plural. The completed examples are: the sheep are eating grass; the farmer has three oxen; he saw two deer in the forest; and the children are playing in the park. The regular plural example is: there are many books on the table.

Transitional Words

  • Earlier, we reached the bus stop.
  • He worked hard. However, he failed.
  • Far away there was a tall tree.
  • Firstly, we must obey them.
  • We played cricket. Then, we had some snacks.

Transitional words join ideas and show order, contrast or distance.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Rhyming Strings
lessons.notes_html:
Completed Rhyming Strings

  • Hat, cat, mat.
  • King, ring, sing.
  • Look, book, hook.
  • Stay, play, day.
  • Tug, jug, rug, bug, hug, mug.

Any word with the same ending sound completes a string, so bat, thing, cook or way can also be correct in their strings.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Paraphrase
lessons.notes_html:
Paraphrase in Own Words

In March, the wind blows strongly and the air smells of spring, as new leaves appear and brave blackbirds sing. In April, gentle showers fall softly and slowly, the earth wakes up from winter, and green plants begin to grow.

A paraphrase keeps the meaning of the original lines and says the same thing in fresh, simple words.

lessons.title: Speaking Practice: A Birthday Party Conversation
lessons.notes_html:
Classroom Practice

The birthday-party conversation between Amina and Faryal, about balloons and tablecloths, is practised aloud in class. It is a speaking activity, so it has no written answer.

lessons.title: Revision Notes: Reading Facts from Units 1 to 3
lessons.notes_html:
Story and Poem Facts Restated

At Taif, the people threw stones at Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) and badly hurt him when he invited them to Islam. He did not curse them; he prayed that their future generations would turn to Islam, and many people of Taif later accepted Islam.

The Muslims were unhappy with the Treaty of Hudaybiyah because the Quraish set very difficult conditions. Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) agreed to the terms for the sake of peace, and this patience later brought success to Islam.

In the Weather poem, February has frosty fogs, winter shivers, and logs burning warm in the fire. February is treated as the coldest month described in the poem, although the poem does not name a coldest month directly.

lessons.title: Revision Notes: Grammar Facts from Units 1 to 3
lessons.notes_html:
Common Gender Nouns

The common gender nouns in the revision sentences are cousin, students, friend, child and cook.

Articles as Completed Sentences

  • I saw an elephant in the zoo.
  • Please give me the book on the table.
  • She bought an orange from the market.
  • I like music very much, with no article before music.
  • The sun rises in the east.

Demonstratives as Completed Sentences

  • This pen in my hand is blue.
  • Those apples on the tree are red.
  • That house across the road is very old.
  • These shoes near the door are mine.
  • The car parked outside is pointed out with that.

Prepositions as Completed Sentences

  • The cat is hiding under the table.
  • She is standing at the bus stop.
  • The birds are flying over the sky.
  • He is sitting between his friends.
  • We will meet on Monday.

Plurals That Do Not Change

Sheep, deer, fish and aircraft keep the same form in the plural: two sheep, two deer, two fish and two aircraft.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Text on Global Warming
lessons.notes_html:
Model Explanatory Text

Global warming means the slow rise in the temperature of the Earth. It happens because smoke from cars and factories and the burning of fuels fill the air with harmful gases that trap heat. Because of global warming, ice melts, seas rise, and the weather becomes hotter with more floods and droughts. We can slow global warming by planting more trees, saving electricity, and using clean energy like sunlight instead of smoke-making fuels.

lessons.title: Reading Notes: How Fossils Form and Why They Matter
lessons.notes_html:
The Lesson in Brief

Fossils are the remains of plants and animals that lived millions of years ago, preserved in rocks that were once mud or sand.

Fossils form in clear steps. When an animal or plant dies, its soft parts decompose quickly, but the hard parts such as bones, shells or teeth can stay. With the passage of time, these hard parts are covered by mud, the mud is pressed down and turns into rock, and the bones become part of the rock.

After discovery, paleontologists record where the fossil was found and the kind of rock it was in, and then the fossil is kept in a museum for study.

Fossils matter to scientists because they teach us about life on Earth long ago, about how plants and animals have changed over time, and about how creatures adapted to their environments. Geologists also use fossils to tell the age of rocks and to match rocks from different places.

Sometimes only the shape of the plant or animal, or its footprints and marks, are left behind. These are called trace fossils.

Key Points

  • Hard parts such as bones, shells and teeth become fossils.
  • Fossils are records of ancient life and of the history of the Earth.
  • Guide fossils help scientists match rocks and judge their age.

lessons.title: Completed Paragraph: Fossils
lessons.notes_html:
The Paragraph Completed

Fossils are very important. They help us learn about life on Earth long ago. Fossils show how plants and animals have changed over time. They help us understand evolution and how creatures adapted to their environments. Fossils also tell us about the history of the Earth and the changes in the environment. Geologists use fossils to tell how old rocks are. Some fossils are good guide fossils. They help scientists match rocks from different places and know which rocks are older or younger.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Each Other, One Another and Pronoun Person
lessons.notes_html:
Each Other and One Another

Use each other for two people and one another for more than two.

  • The two sisters love each other.
  • The players in the team encourage one another.
  • The teacher and the student respect each other.

Pronoun Person

  • She is third person.
  • I is first person.
  • You is second person.
  • They is third person.
  • We is first person.

The first person is the speaker, the second person is the listener, and the third person is the one spoken about.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Interrogative Pronouns, Synonyms and Antonyms
lessons.notes_html:
Interrogative Pronouns in Completed Sentences

  • Who is knocking at the gate.
  • Whose bag is lying on the floor.
  • What is your favourite subject, stated as a fact pattern for practice.
  • Which of these pens is yours, stated as a fact pattern for practice.
  • Whom did she call yesterday, stated as a fact pattern for practice.

In class these five pronouns are practised inside full spoken sentences; here they are recorded as the correct word for each gap.

Synonyms and Antonyms

  • Happy: synonym glad, antonym sad.
  • Small: synonym little, antonym big.
  • Fast: synonym quick, antonym slow.
  • Light: synonym bright, antonym dark; for weight, the antonym is heavy.
  • Big: synonym large, antonym small.
  • Early: synonym soon, antonym late.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Imperatives, Infinitives and Adverbs
lessons.notes_html:
Imperative Sentences as Models

  • Do not touch the hot pan.
  • Please open the window.
  • Please keep quiet.
  • Walk faster, please.
  • Please bring me a pen.

An imperative sentence gives a command or a polite request and usually begins with the verb.

Infinitives as Completed Sentences

  • I like to swim in the sea.
  • He wants to become a doctor.
  • We need to finish our homework.
  • They decided to visit the museum.
  • She loves to dance at parties.

Adverbs and the Words They Qualify

  • Peacefully qualifies the verb slept.
  • Really qualifies the adjective hard.
  • Extremely qualifies the adverb politely.
  • Very qualifies the adjective beautiful.
  • Too qualifies the adverb quickly.

Kinds of Adverbs: Model Sentences

  • Manner: he runs quickly.
  • Time: we will go shopping tomorrow.
  • Place: the children are playing outside.
  • Frequency: she never forgets her homework.
  • Manner: the old man walked slowly.

Other adverbs of the same kind are also correct in these model sentences.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Composition on My Best Teacher
lessons.notes_html:
Five-Paragraph Model

Paragraph 1, Introduction: Everyone needs a good teacher in life. My best teacher is Miss Fatima, who teaches us English in Class 4.

Paragraph 2, Qualities: She is kind, patient and honest, and she explains every lesson in a simple and clear way.

Paragraph 3, Activities: We read stories, learn new words and play learning games in her class, and she helps me whenever I face a difficulty.

Paragraph 4, Importance: She is important to me because she encourages me to work hard and to speak with confidence.

Paragraph 5, Conclusion: Miss Fatima is not only my teacher but also like a kind guide, and I am lucky to be her student.

The writing process in the unit is brainstorming first, then a mind map, then a first draft.

lessons.title: Speaking Practice: Expressing Needs and Feelings
lessons.notes_html:
Classroom Practice

The conversation for expressing needs and feelings, between Shahista and her friend, is practised aloud in class. It is a speaking activity, so it has no written answer.

lessons.title: Reading Notes: The King Who Cared for His People
lessons.notes_html:
The Story in Brief

In a land with a strange law, a king rules for only three years and is then left in a dark forest, until one brave man changes everything by caring for his people.

The strange law said that whoever became king could rule for only three years. After that, he would be taken into a dark, dense forest and left there to die.

People were afraid to accept the throne because of this cruel law, so no one dared to sit on the throne.

The first clever order of the new king was for his soldiers to build a wide road through the forest. The soldiers worked hard, and soon a clear path appeared through the forest.

After three years, the people refused to send him into the forest. Unlike the kings before him, who only cared for their palaces, he had cared for the people: he solved their problems, dug wells, built hospitals and schools, planted trees and gave them a better life, so they could not let him go.

The lesson of the story is that a true leader cares for his people instead of only himself. A ruler who solves problems, gives justice and works for the welfare of the people wins their love and respect, and good leadership brings a better life for everyone.

Key Points

  • Wise planning can turn a place of fear into a place of life.
  • People protect a leader who first protects them.
  • Real leadership is service, justice and care.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Confused Words, Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.notes_html:
Two, Too and To; There, Their and They Are

  • I have two dogs.
  • We are going to the market.
  • She wants to play cricket too.
  • The students are sitting over there.
  • This is their classroom.
  • They are very excited for the trip, written in its short form in the exercise.

Prefixes

  • Legal with a prefix becomes illegal, meaning not legal.
  • Correct with a prefix becomes incorrect, meaning not correct.
  • Do with a prefix becomes redo, meaning do again.

Suffixes

  • Teach with a suffix becomes teacher, a person who teaches.
  • Play with a suffix becomes playful, full of play.
  • Kind with a suffix becomes kindness, the quality of being kind.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Phonics Facts
lessons.notes_html:
Vowels, Doubling and Silent Letters

Short vowels: the e in pet, the u in sun, the o in hop and the i in sit. Long vowels: the a in cake, the i in bike, the oa in boat and the ee in seed.

When -ing is added after a short vowel and one consonant, the final consonant doubles: tapping, jogging, getting and clapping.

Silent letters: the w in write, the b in thumb, the b in comb and the k in knee.

Word Families and Digraphs

  • The -at family: cat, bat, hat, sat, mat.
  • The -ot family: hot, lot, pot, not, dot.
  • The -ake family: bake, lake, make, take, cake.
  • The letter y sounds like i in cry, fly and my, and like e in happy, baby and funny.
  • Digraphs: sh in fish, th in thin, wh in what and ch in chat.
  • Vowel digraphs complete the words rain, boat and seed.
  • Blends match the words blue, star, crab and queen.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Narrative
lessons.notes_html:
Model Narrative with Beginning, Middle and End

Last Sunday, my family and I went to the park in the morning. First, we walked under the tall trees and my little brother ran to the swings. Then, we played cricket together and ate sandwiches under a shady tree. Finally, we returned home in the evening, tired but happy, and I told my grandmother everything about our lovely day.

A narrative follows a clear sequence of events: a beginning that sets the scene, a middle with the main events, and an end that closes the story.

lessons.title: Speaking Practice: Everyday Conversations
lessons.notes_html:
Classroom Practice

The four everyday conversations, covering introducing, giving directions, making a call and making a request, are role-played in pairs in class. They are speaking activities, so they have no written answers.

lessons.title: Reading Notes: A Little World Built with Love
lessons.notes_html:
The Poem in Brief

This poem by Emily Dickinson calls the family a little world, built with love and care, where members learn to share and kindness is the rule.

The poem describes a family as a little world and a place of comfort, hope and cheer, where the family stands near in laughter, tears and every day.

The family is built with love and care. Family members learn to share, and kindness is the important rule they live by.

The family stays close together in laughter, tears and every day, standing near through both happy and sad times.

Key Points

  • A family is a small world of comfort, hope and cheer.
  • Love and care are the building blocks of a family.
  • Sharing and kindness keep a family close in all times.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Abbreviations and Compound Words
lessons.notes_html:
Abbreviations in Full

  • Wed. means Wednesday.
  • Nov. means November.
  • Ms. means Miss, used for a woman without stating marital status.
  • a.m. means ante meridiem, before noon, the morning.
  • Fri. means Friday.

Compound Words and Their Meanings

  • Sunflower: a tall yellow flower that turns towards the sun.
  • Rainbow: a colourful arc seen in the sky after rain.
  • Toothbrush: a small brush used to clean the teeth.
  • Snowman: a figure made of snow, usually with a carrot nose.
  • Football: a game played by kicking a ball with the feet.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Regular and Irregular Verbs
lessons.notes_html:
Regular Verbs as Completed Sentences

  • She walked to school yesterday.
  • They are playing football now.
  • He always helps his mother.

Regular verbs form their past forms in a regular way, mostly by adding -ed or -d.

Irregular Verbs as Completed Sentences

  • She went to the park yesterday.
  • He has eaten all the cake.
  • They wrote a letter last night.

Irregular verbs change their form in the past, so their forms are learned by heart: go becomes went, eat becomes eaten, and write becomes wrote.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Editing a Paragraph on My Family
lessons.notes_html:
First Draft and Edited Draft

First draft: My family is big and nice. We live in a house. We eat food together. My family is good.

Edited draft: My family is large and loving. We live together in a comfortable house near the market. Every evening, we share a delicious meal and talk about our day. My parents are caring and my brothers are playful. I am lucky because my family is wonderful and always supports me.

Editing improves a paragraph by choosing stronger describing words and adding clear details.

lessons.title: Speaking and Punctuation Practice
lessons.notes_html:
Classroom Practice

The conversation between Ahmed and Aslam about borrowing colour pencils is practised in pairs. The class also re-reads the unit and highlights the punctuation marks used. Both are classroom activities, so they have no written answers.

lessons.title: Revision Notes: Reading Facts from Units 4 to 6
lessons.notes_html:
Facts Restated

Trace fossils are the shapes, footprints or marks left behind by a plant or animal after its body decomposed. They show where an animal walked or lived, even though the body itself is gone.

Fossils are important because they teach us about life on Earth long ago, about how plants and animals changed over time, and about how creatures adapted to their environments. They also tell us about the history of the Earth and help scientists tell the age of rocks.

Real happiness never comes from teasing a person or an animal, because teasing hurts others and makes them sad. Real happiness comes from kindness, sharing and caring for others. No lesson passage in Units 4 to 6 discusses teasing directly, so this point is answered from the values taught across the book, as the flags chapter explains.

In the poem, a family is a little world and a place of comfort, hope and cheer, standing near in laughter, tears and every day. The family is built with love and care.

lessons.title: Revision Notes: Grammar Facts from Units 4 to 6
lessons.notes_html:
Interrogative Pronouns

The correct pronoun for each revision gap is recorded here in order: Who for the person knocking at the gate, Whose for the bag on the floor, What for the favourite subject, Which for choosing among pens, and Whom for the person called yesterday.

Synonyms and Antonyms

  • Happy: glad and sad.
  • Small: little and big.
  • Fast: quick and slow.
  • Light: bright and dark.
  • Big: large and small.
  • Early: soon and late.

Confused Words as Completed Sentences

  • I have two dogs.
  • We are going to the market.
  • She wants to play cricket too.
  • The students are sitting over there.
  • This is their classroom.
  • They are very excited for the trip, in short form in the exercise.

Compound Words and Abbreviations

The compound words are sunflower, rainbow, toothbrush, snowman and football, with the meanings given in Unit 6. The abbreviations stand for Wednesday, November, Miss, ante meridiem and Friday.

chapters.title: Unit 7: Importance of Discipline in Life

lessons.title: Reading Notes: Discipline in Nature, School and Nation
lessons.notes_html:
The Lesson in Brief

Discipline means following rules and principles in an orderly way, and without it no one can get success in life.

Everything in nature follows rules: the sun, the moon and the stars move by fixed laws, and the organs of the body work in an orderly way.

Life becomes unsafe and difficult when people do not follow rules. A driver who breaks traffic rules causes accidents, a family system is disturbed when members do not do their duties, and nations that did not follow discipline became weak.

Discipline helps students in clear ways: it helps them to be on time and to stay calm, and it teaches them to do important work first. It also builds a positive attitude, improves performance step by step, and builds a healthy mind and body.

A team whose players do not obey their captain loses the match. A disciplined team can win.

Pakistan can become a great country when its people are disciplined: following traffic rules and staying disciplined in school, in classrooms and in daily life.

Key Points

  • Discipline is orderly obedience to good rules.
  • Nature itself works in a disciplined way.
  • Discipline brings safety, success and national strength.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Simple Present Tense
lessons.notes_html:
The Rule

The simple present tense describes daily habits and general truths. With he, she or it, the verb usually takes -s or -es.

Worked Examples as Completed Sentences

  • She drinks milk every night.
  • The earth moves around the sun.
  • They go to school by bus.
  • My mother cooks very well.
  • We speak English in class.
  • The teacher checks our homework.
  • A dog barks loudly.
  • Farmers grow crops in the fields.
  • The moon shines at night.
  • My brother helps me with homework.

lessons.title: Reading Strategy and Speaking Practice
lessons.notes_html:
Five Strategies for Unfamiliar Words

Unfamiliar words can be tackled in five ways: sounding the word out, splitting it into syllables, using analogy with known words, studying its prefixes and suffixes, and guessing from context.

Classroom Practice

Dialogue 1, about borrowing a pen, and Dialogue 2, about passing the salt, are practised in pairs. A group discussion on the importance of discipline in school is also a classroom activity. These speaking tasks have no written answers.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Speech Bubbles in Order
lessons.notes_html:
Model Conversation

One friend suggests playing football. The other friend agrees warmly and calls it a good idea. The first friend then suggests playing at once.

The bubbles are filled with a short, polite agreement to play, arranged in a sensible order for a conversation between friends.

lessons.title: Reading Notes: Small Acts of Politeness
lessons.notes_html:
The Poem in Brief

The poem shows politeness in small daily acts: a quiet nod, a gentle please, doors held open, thank-yous whispered, and a smile shared in the eyes of strangers.

Polite words in the poem include please, thank-you and the reply given after thanks. The poem also mentions a quiet nod, soft tones and a shared smile.

Thanks is the right response when someone helps. Thanks is whispered, and the reply is spoken back with warmth and gentle manners.

Being polite puts a heart at ease and plants a peace that remains. Gentle manners bind wounds, soothe fears, and make love felt in passing years.

Good manners in the poem include holding doors open for others, walking with slow footsteps and soft tones, and forgiving small mistakes when tempers flare.

Daily politeness matters because gentle manners weave the air that binds people together. Loud praise and grand affairs may be forgotten, but politeness soothes fears, keeps peace, and makes love felt in passing years.

Key Points

  • Politeness lives in small acts done every day.
  • Thanks and its kind reply keep hearts at ease.
  • Gentle manners build lasting peace between people.

lessons.title: Listening Notes: A Visit to the Zoo
lessons.notes_html:
Facts from the Listening Passage

  • The class of Ali went to the zoo.
  • The children saw monkeys jumping and playing, a lion in its cage, and elephants.
  • The elephants were eating sugarcane.
  • At the end, the teacher gave the children some snacks, and they returned home happily.
  • The story is mostly about a class visit to the city zoo.

This is the one listening activity in the book that carries its own passage with set facts, so its facts are recorded here in full.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Contractions and Alphabetical Order
lessons.notes_html:
Contractions

  • Cannot becomes can’t.
  • Will not becomes won’t.
  • Did not becomes didn’t.
  • Could not becomes couldn’t.
  • Should not becomes shouldn’t.
  • Is not becomes isn’t.
  • They are becomes they’re.
  • We have becomes we’ve.

An apostrophe in a contraction marks the place where letters have been dropped.

Alphabetical Order

The words in alphabetical order are: April, apply, apron, chair, chain, chalk, change, scarf, school. April comes before apply because the letters pr come before pp at the second and third letters. Chair, chain, chalk and change are ordered by their later letters.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Phrase, Sentence, Subject, Verb and Object
lessons.notes_html:
Phrase and Sentence

A phrase has meaning but no complete idea, while a sentence has a subject and a predicate and gives a complete idea. In the worked set, the phrases are the groups about running through the park, the old wooden bridge, a basket of apples, dancing under the moonlight and speaking no words. The sentences are the complete statements about reading mystery novels, the barking dog, the beach trip, the repaired chair and the rising sun.

Subject and Verb

  • The baby is the subject and cries is the verb.
  • The sun is the subject and shines is the verb.
  • They is the subject and sat is the verb.
  • She is the subject and dances is the verb.
  • The bird is the subject and sings is the verb.

Subject, Verb and Object

  • She sings a song: subject She, verb sings, object a song.
  • They opened the door: subject They, verb opened, object the door.
  • The child ate an apple: subject The child, verb ate, object an apple.
  • He learned the lesson: subject He, verb learned, object the lesson.
  • We played the game: subject We, verb played, object the game.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Present Continuous Tense and Modal Verbs
lessons.notes_html:
Present Continuous: Worked Examples

  • I am eating lunch now.
  • The children are playing outside.
  • She is writing a letter at the moment.
  • We are learning English in class.
  • The baby is sleeping in the bed.
  • They are watching TV right now.
  • He is running in the park.
  • My friends are sitting in the library.
  • The teacher is explaining the lesson.
  • You are reading a book at the moment.

The present continuous tense uses am, is or are with the -ing form for actions happening now.

Modal Verbs as Completed Sentences

  • Can introduces the swimming ability sentence.
  • You should not waste food.
  • We may go to the zoo tomorrow.
  • Can introduces the offer of help.
  • He could play football when he was young.
  • Can introduces the offer to carry the bag.
  • You should pray five times a day.
  • It might rain later in the evening.
  • May introduces the polite request about a morning call.
  • A rich person in the imagined sentence would buy a big house.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Invitation
lessons.notes_html:
Model Invitation

A.B.C, City, 12 September 2025. Dear Fehmeeda, I hope you and your family are fine. I have my birthday after a few days, and I have invited my friends to my birthday party on 30 October 2025. I want to invite you and your family to attend my birthday. I hope you all will join this event. Give my regards to your family. Your best friend, Firdos.

A good invitation gives the event, the date, a warm request to attend, and regards for the family.

lessons.title: Reading Notes: Mehrgarh, the Oldest Settlement
lessons.notes_html:
The Lesson in Brief

On a museum visit, Sarah tells Ahmad about Mehrgarh in the Kachhi district of Balochistan, one of the oldest known settlements in the world, dating back to around 7000 BC. Civilization in South Asia began there, long before the Indus Valley Civilization.

The people of Mehrgarh survived without modern technology because they were intelligent. They made stone tools, built homes with mud bricks, and stored food in large clay pots. They grew wheat and barley, raised goats and sheep, and over time started using copper and crafting more advanced tools.

They buried their dead with belongings because they believed in an afterlife. Their burial sites tell us a lot about their culture and beliefs.

Mehrgarh influenced the Indus Valley Civilization because the early ideas of agriculture, trade, art and community living all started there and later shaped that civilization. Its people laid the foundation for future generations.

Its craftsmen were highly skilled. They made jewellery from stones, shells and bones, and they grew cotton and spun it into threads to make clothes, long before many other civilizations.

Key Points

  • Mehrgarh dates back to around 7000 BC.
  • Farming, building and craft skills began there very early.
  • Mehrgarh laid the foundation of the Indus Valley Civilization.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Simile and Metaphor
lessons.notes_html:
The Rule

A simile compares two things with like or as. A metaphor states the comparison directly, without like or as.

Worked Examples Classified

  • A simile: skin compared with cotton using as soft as.
  • A metaphor: a classroom called a beehive of activity.
  • A simile: running compared with the wind using like.
  • A metaphor: time called a thief.
  • A simile: a voice compared with the ocean using as deep as.
  • A metaphor: a little brother called a monkey.
  • A simile: a night compared with coal using as dark as.
  • A metaphor: life called a journey with many roads.
  • A simile: snow compared with a white blanket using like.
  • A metaphor: eyes called stars shining in the night sky.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Poetic Devices and Joining Words
lessons.notes_html:
Poetic Devices Classified

  • The repeated hot, hot, hot line is repetition, used for effect.
  • The smiling moon line is marked as a sensory image of sight among the five labels offered, although its exact device is personification; the flags chapter explains this honestly.
  • Wall and ball form a rhyme.
  • As tall as a giraffe is a simile.
  • The music beat that made hands clap shows rhythm.

Joining Words as Completed Sentences

  • I like to play football and cricket.
  • Ali was tired but he finished his homework.
  • Milk or water is the choice offered in the practice sentence.
  • Sara is smart but lazy.
  • It was raining, so we took an umbrella.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Sentence Types, Present Perfect and Clauses
lessons.notes_html:
Sentence Types Classified

Declarative sentences state facts, interrogative sentences ask, imperative sentences command or request, and exclamatory sentences show strong feeling. In the worked set: the shining stars sentence is declarative; the time sentence is interrogative; kindness to animals is imperative; the beautiful flowers sentence is exclamatory; the movie sentence is declarative; helping a brother is imperative; the rainbow sentence is interrogative; the storybook sentence is declarative; the hot pan warning is imperative with strong force; and the amazing job sentence is exclamatory.

Present Perfect: Worked Examples

  • I have eaten breakfast already.
  • She has finished her work just now.
  • They have not arrived yet, in contracted form in the exercise.
  • The seen form completes the movie sentence: seen.
  • We have started the lesson already.
  • He has just called his friend.
  • The completed form for homework is completed.
  • I have read this story already.
  • She has just left the room.
  • They have not decided yet, in contracted form in the exercise.

Main and Subordinate Clauses

  • Main: she was sad. Subordinate: because her toy was broken.
  • Main: I will call you. Subordinate: when I reach home.
  • Main: he did not come to school. Subordinate: as he was sick.
  • Main: we cannot go outside. Subordinate: if it rains.
  • Main: I was surprised. Subordinate: that he passed the test.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Text on the Uses of Mobile Phones
lessons.notes_html:
Model Informative Text

Introduction: Mobile phones are very useful in our daily life.

Body: First, we can call and message our family and friends from anywhere, which keeps us connected. Second, we can learn many things on a mobile phone by reading, watching lessons and searching for information. Third, mobile phones help us take photos, check the time and find directions on a map.

Conclusion: In short, mobile phones are useful tools for talking, learning and daily work, but we should use them for a limited time and for good purposes.

lessons.title: Speaking Practice: Group Presentations
lessons.notes_html:
Classroom Practice

Group presentations follow four steps from the unit: read widely, look for common themes, compare, and connect facts, then share the prepared information clearly with an audience. This is a classroom activity, so it has no written answer.

lessons.title: Revision Notes: Grammar Facts from Units 7 to 9
lessons.notes_html:
Simple Present Forms in Order

The correct simple present forms are: drinks, moves, go, cooks, speak, checks, barks, grow, shines and helps.

Subject, Verb and Object

  • She sings a song: She, sings, a song.
  • They opened the door: They, opened, the door.
  • The child ate an apple: The child, ate, an apple.
  • He learned the lesson: He, learned, the lesson.
  • We played the game: We, played, the game.

Sentence Types

The ten revision sentences classify in the same order as in Unit 9: declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamatory, declarative, imperative, interrogative, declarative, imperative, exclamatory.

Present Perfect Forms in Order

The correct present perfect forms are: eaten, finished, arrived, seen and started.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Invitation Revisited
lessons.notes_html:
Model Invitation

A.B.C, City, 12 September 2025. My dear friend, I hope you and your family are fine. I have my birthday after a few days, and I have invited my friends to my birthday party. I want to invite you and your family to attend my birthday. I hope you all will join this event. Give my regards to all your family. Your best friend, Firdos.

chapters.title: Unit 10: Planting Trees is a Continuous Charity

lessons.title: Reading Notes: Trees, Charity and Clean Air
lessons.notes_html:
The Lesson in Brief

Planting trees is Sadaqa e Jariyah: a good deed that keeps giving reward even after the death of a person.

Sadaqa e Jariyah is continuous charity: good deeds that give reward to a person even after death. When a person dies, deeds stop except for three things: continuous charity, useful knowledge, and a faithful child who prays for the parent.

Planting a tree is Sadaqa e Jariyah because the planter keeps receiving reward from it. Trees protect us from climate change and diseases, clean the air, give oxygen and food, and keep the earth balanced, so their benefit continues long after planting.

The main cause of air pollution is smoke from cars, factories and burning waste. Pollution causes problems like global warming, acid rain, ozone damage and diseases.

According to experts, 25 percent of the total land of a country should be covered by forests. In Pakistan, only 2 to 3 percent of land has forests, which is a very low ratio, so planting trees is the duty of every citizen.

Trees provide oxygen, which is necessary for humans and animals, and plants and trees also clean the air by absorbing pollution.

Key Points

  • A planted tree keeps benefiting people for many years.
  • Forests should cover about a quarter of a country.
  • Clean air depends on more trees and less smoke.

lessons.title: Speaking Notes: Debate and Steps for Planting a Tree
lessons.notes_html:
Debate Practice

Debates argue for or against a topic using evidence, following the debate steps in the unit. Debate is a classroom speaking activity, so it has no written answer.

Steps for Planting a Tree from the Lesson

Choose and clear the place, dig a hole, bring a plant from a nursery, remove the plastic bag, put the plant in the hole, cover the roots with soil, add more soil around the stem, water gently, and protect the plant from harm and disease.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Simple Past Tense
lessons.notes_html:
Past Verbs Identified

The past-tense verbs in the worked sentences are: watched, visited, played, cleaned, studied, cooked, laughed, opened, travelled and enjoyed. Each verb shows an action that happened and finished in the past.

Simple Past as Completed Sentences

  • Yesterday, I went to school late.
  • She bought a new dress last week.
  • They played cricket in the ground.
  • We ate pizza at the restaurant.
  • He washed his car in the morning.
  • The children watched cartoons yesterday.
  • My mother made tea for us.
  • I read a storybook last night.
  • The dog ran after the cat.
  • We visited the museum last Friday.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Be-Verb Sentences, Apostrophes and Contractions
lessons.notes_html:
Be Verbs in Completed Sentences

  • Am I your friend, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • Is she your English teacher, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • Are they coming to school today, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • Was it hot yesterday, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • Are you busy right now, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • Were the children happy at the party, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • Is this your pencil, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • Are we late for the meeting, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • Is he your classmate, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • Were you at home last night, stated as a completed pattern sentence.

Present forms am, is and are pair with present time, and past forms was and were pair with past time.

Apostrophes Corrected

  • This is my brother’s book.
  • The dog’s tail is very long.
  • The teacher’s pen is on the table.
  • The children’s toys are in the box.
  • The cook’s pies smell delicious.

Contractions as Completed Sentences

  • I’m going to the park.
  • They’re playing football.
  • It’s raining outside.
  • I’ve written a story.
  • He’s studying day and night.
  • We can’t attend the party.
  • She’s cooked food.
  • Don’t come late in the class.
  • We’ll play football tomorrow.
  • I’m going to Lahore.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Imagery, Character and -ly Adverbs
lessons.notes_html:
Model Imagery Sentences

  • Sight: the bright red flowers danced in the wind.
  • Touch: the petals felt smooth and silky under her fingers.
  • Sound: birds sang sweetly in the trees.
  • Character: the gentle voice and caring nature of Ayesha made her seem like someone who always spread happiness.

-ly Adverbs as Completed Sentences

  • The baby cried loudly.
  • She sang the song beautifully.
  • He walked slowly into the dark street.
  • The teacher spoke kindly to the students.
  • They finished their work quickly.

Other -ly adverbs that fit a sentence are also correct.

lessons.title: Reading Notes: A Useful Network with Limits
lessons.notes_html:
The Lesson in Brief

The entire world is connected with one network, the internet, which has made human life easy but must be used within a limit.

The internet has made life easy because people can solve many issues with a few clicks. We can find information on any topic, learn anything, run a business, and contact anyone quickly.

People stay in contact easily through social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, where they interact with friends and family and share views and opinions.

The biggest advantage of the internet is access to information. Anything we need to know can be searched online, and there are good articles, videos and images on every topic.

Online games carry real disadvantages. Young people can become addicted to social media and games, which harms health and education. Addiction affects both physical and mental health directly, and fake news and violence are also common on social media.

A sensible personal limit is about one hour a day for study and for talking to family. This time answer is personal, so every student writes an honest personal answer in class; the flags chapter explains this point.

Key Points

  • Information is the biggest gift of the internet.
  • Connection with family and friends is quick and easy online.
  • Addiction harms health and studies, so limits matter.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Feeling Words and Future Tense
lessons.notes_html:
Feeling Words as Completed Sentences

  • The mouse was terrified when the cat chased it.
  • Saima was downhearted after losing her favourite toy.
  • Aslam felt embarrassed when everyone laughed at his mistake.
  • The players were delighted to hear that they had won the match.
  • The man was disgruntled about the poor service at the restaurant.

Future Forms as Completed Sentences

  • I will call you in the evening.
  • We will help our teacher with the work.
  • She is going to visit her friend tomorrow.
  • Shall we go to the zoo today, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • They are going to play cricket on Sunday.
  • He will study hard for the test.
  • I shall return the book to you soon.
  • We are going to watch a movie tonight.
  • Shall I open the window, stated as a completed pattern sentence.
  • She is going to buy a new dress next week.

Where both will and the going-to form fit, the planned-action form is given.

Dictation Practice

The dictation paragraph begins with the line about the biggest advantage of the internet being access to information. Its spellings are learned from the unit paragraph.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Transitional Words in a Morning Story
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Examples as Completed Sentences

  • Firstly, Ali woke up early in the morning.
  • He brushed his teeth and next ate breakfast.
  • Later on, his mother called him to get ready for school.
  • The school was nearby, so he walked there quickly.
  • Suddenly, he met his friends in the classroom.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Opinion Piece
lessons.notes_html:
Model Opinion Piece

The book I read is a storybook about a kind king. In my opinion, it is a very good book because it teaches us to care for others. I like it because the king helps poor people, and I also like its simple and clear language. Overall, I believe this book is a useful and interesting book for every student.

An opinion piece states a clear view, gives reasons for it, and ends with an overall judgement.

lessons.title: Speaking Practice: Drama in Small Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Classroom Practice

A short drama or play is enacted in small groups of three to five members: the group chooses a simple theme, assigns roles, writes simple dialogues and performs in front of the class. Drama is a classroom activity, so it has no written answer.

lessons.title: Reading Notes: Following the Wind
lessons.notes_html:
The Poem in Brief

This poem by A. A. Milne presents a poet who cannot keep up with the wind, yet thinks that letting go of a kite string could show where the wind goes.

Rhyming words from the poem include knows and goes, can and ran, kite and night, and blew and too. The poem opens and closes with the same knows and goes rhyme. Its rhyme pattern is loose in the middle stanzas, as the flags chapter explains.

The speed of the wind is explained through flight: the wind flies from somewhere as fast as it can, and the poet could not keep up with it, not even by running.

The poet imagines learning the path of the wind through a kite. By no longer holding the string, the kite would blow with the wind for a day and a night, and finding the kite would show where the wind had been going.

Nobody can tell where the wind comes from. The poem repeats this mystery at its opening and its close.

A model personal response describes flying a kite with a brother on a windy evening: the wind pulled the kite high, tightened the string, and made the kite dance and dive, teaching that the wind is powerful and the string must be held tightly. Every student writes a personal experience in class.

Key Points

  • The wind is invisible, fast and mysterious.
  • A free kite can reveal the path of the wind.
  • Rhyme gives the poem its music and its frame.

lessons.title: Listening Notes: Stress and Intonation
lessons.notes_html:
Facts from the Listening Activity

  • The market sentence is a statement with a falling voice.
  • The park sentence rises at the end and works as an invitation to respond.
  • The sitting instruction is a command with a falling voice.
  • The cake sentence is a statement with a falling voice, with stress on the denial.
  • The homework sentence rises at the end and works as an invitation to respond.

Statements and commands usually end with a falling voice, while sentences seeking a response usually rise.

lessons.title: Grammar Notes: Similes and Direct Speech
lessons.notes_html:
Similes as Completed Sentences

  • The night was as black as coal.
  • He is as brave as a lion.
  • She sings like a nightingale.
  • My grandmother’s hair is as white as snow, with the possessive form used in written work.
  • He runs like a cheetah.

Direct Speech

Direct speech gives the exact words spoken, written inside quotation marks. In the worked set, the quoted parts are the tiredness statement of Ali, the ice-cream sentence of Sara, the book-opening instruction of the teacher, the car warning shouted by Ahmed, and the grandparents visit sentence of the children.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Application for Fee Concession
lessons.notes_html:
Model Application

To, The Principal, ABC School, Quetta. Subject: Application for fee concession. Respected Sir or Madam, I am writing to request a concession in my school fee. My father is the only earning member of our family, and it is difficult for him to pay the full fee along with our other expenses. I am a hardworking student of Class 4 and I always try my best in studies. I kindly request you to grant me a fee concession. I shall be very thankful to you. Thank you for your favour. Yours faithfully, Ali Khan, Class 4. Dated: 09-09-2025.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Cinquain and Paraphrase
lessons.notes_html:
Model Cinquain on Tree

Tree. Tall, green. Growing, shading, giving. Gives us shade and fruit. Friend.

A cinquain follows the pattern of one word, two words, three words, four words and one word.

Model Paraphrase

Nobody can tell me where the wind comes from or where it goes to. No one in the world knows the answer to this mystery.

lessons.title: Revision Notes: Grammar Facts from Units 10 to 12
lessons.notes_html:
Be-Verb Forms in Order

The correct forms are: Am, Is, Are, Was, Are, Were, Is and Are.

Simple Past Forms in Order

The correct simple past forms are: played, ate, washed, watched, made and read.

Feeling Words in Order

Similes as Completed Sentences

  • The night was as black as coal.
  • He is as brave as a lion.
  • She sings like a nightingale.
  • My grandmother’s hair is as white as snow, with the possessive form used in written work.
  • He runs like a cheetah.

lessons.title: Writing Notes: Model Application Revisited
lessons.notes_html:
Model Application

To, The Principal, ABC School, Quetta. Subject: Application for fee concession. Respected Sir or Madam, I am writing to request a concession in my school fee, as my father is the only earning member of our family and finds it difficult to pay the full fee. chapters.title: A Note on Flagged Items in the Printed Book

lessons.title: Honest Notes on Open and Unclear Items
lessons.notes_html:
Nothing Invented

Nothing in this chapter is invented as book content. These are the places where the notes had to use judgement because the book itself is open, unclear or silent. All other notes follow the lesson text and the grammar rules taught in each unit.

Unit 1 Word Bank

The word bank has ten words for ten blanks, but the fit is not unique for every blank. The notes give one sensible model set and leave carefully unused. Another fitting bank word in a blank should also be accepted.

Unit 3 Coldest Month

The poem does not name any month as the coldest. The notes answer February because February carries frosty fogs and shivering winter in the poem. This is an inference from the description, not a line quoted from the poem. The same point applies in the first revision chapter.

Open Adverb Blanks

The adverb-kind activity in Unit 4 and the -ly adverb activity in Unit 10 have no single correct word. Any adverb of the hinted kind, or any fitting -ly adverb, is correct, so the notes give model answers only.

Unit 9 Smiling Moon

The smiling moon sentence is personification, which is not one of the five labels the activity offers. Among the offered labels, the notes mark it as a sensory image of sight and flag that the fit is imperfect. The other four items are clear: repetition, rhyme, simile and rhythm.

Unit 11 Personal Time

The internet-time point is personal and has no book answer. The notes give a model of a limited time, about one hour a day for study, and students write their own honest answers.

Unit 12 Rhymes

The rhyme pattern of the poem is loose in the middle stanzas. The notes give the clear pairs and note the near rhymes rather than forcing a perfect pair for every line.

Revision on Teasing

No lesson passage in Units 4 to 6 discusses teasing directly. The revision note answers from the values taught across the book: teasing hurts others, and real happiness comes from kindness.

Speaking, Listening and Drama Activities

Conversations, dialogues, group discussions, listening passages and drama enactments are classroom speaking activities with no written answers in the book. The notes record what to practise and, for the zoo visit in Unit 8, record the facts of the listening passage. No written answers are invented for pure practice tasks.

The Honorific

The book prints Arabic honorific calligraphy after the name of the Prophet. These notes use (PBUH) in plain text because the English notes font cannot reliably print the calligraphic form.

Glossary

The glossary at the end of the textbook is a word list with no solved items, so it carries no separate notes chapter.
